newsitem.title: UNITED NATIONS: U.S. set to veto second term for Boutros-Ghali. [CORRECTED 22:55 GMT]
newsitem.headline: U.S. set to veto second term for Boutros-Ghali. [CORRECTED 22:55 GMT]

text.p: The Security Council began consultations on Monday to nominate a secretary-general, with U.S. Ambassador Madeleine Albright armed with instructions to block a second term for Boutros Boutros-Ghali.

Egypt's Ambassador Nabil Elaraby said he expected a resolution in favour of Boutros-Ghali would be put before the 15-member council later on Monday and that all delegations except the United States would vote for it.

"There will be 14 votes on record in favour. They (the members) told me," Elaraby told Reuters. The resolution, drawn up by Egypt, Botswana and Guinea-Bissau -- the council's three African members -- has a total of nine sponsors so far, diplomats said.

The purpose of the resolution is to put on record the council's overwhelming support for Boutros-Ghali and in the process isolate the United States, which has been strongly criticised for its position on Boutros-Ghali and for owing $1.4 billion in dues and peacekeeping contributions.

Albright's spokesman, James Rubin, said she had received written instructions from Washington to oppose Boutros-Ghali's candidacy. He said the U.S. Congress had lost confidence in Boutros-Ghali and his re-election "would make it virtually impossible for us to obtain the hundreds of millions of dollars that we need to pay back the United Nations."
Several council members privately said they doubted the Republican-led Congress would provide the funds anyway.

The consultations were largely to determine whether there had been any change of heart on the part of the United States, which for months has been calling for new leadership to carry out reform of the world body.

If and when a veto is cast, council members would again consult and give preference to other African candidates on the grounds that if, contrary to U.N. practice, a secretary-general was denied a second term, he should at least be succeeded by someone from his region of the world.

Diplomats said British Ambassador Sir John Weston (corrects name), evidently fearing a deadlock, was reported to have told the council his country would vote for Boutros-Ghali but the 15-member body should consider its next moves in light of the U.S. position.
Italy was said to have spoken of a compromise term instead of the usual five years.

During a recess, the three African members of the council -- Egypt, Botswana and Guinea-Bissau -- notified Boutros-Ghali that there had been no change in the U.S. position. One member of the group said he received the news in a "dignified" manner.
Boutros-Ghali's current term expires on Dec. 31.
Most council members declined comment on their way into the consultations but Chinese Ambassador Qin Huasun told reporters his country backed Boutros Ghali's candidacy.
Rubin, for his part, went on the offensive against those who believed the United States might have a change of heart after its Nov. 5 elections.

"Those countries who refused to discuss this issue over the last six months have done a disservice to the United Nations. We tried to create a process by which there would have been adequate time over the last six months to discuss alternatives. But some believed, based on a misunderstanding of American politics, that the president (Clinton) would change his mind after the election," Rubin said.
